depletions.mechanism: Statins inhibit HMG-CoA reductase, the same early step of the mevalonate pathway the body uses to make ubiquinone (CoQ10). Placebo-controlled trials, pooled in a meta-analysis, show statin therapy lowers CoQ10 concentrations measured in blood.
depletions.clinical_impact: Whether that lower blood level causes the muscle symptoms some people report on statins is not established, and it does not by itself indicate a tissue deficiency. Trials of CoQ10 supplements for statin-related muscle symptoms disagree: some pooled analyses report improvement, others find no benefit over placebo.
depletions.recommendation: Statins can lower circulating CoQ10 levels. It is uncertain whether this contributes to muscle symptoms or whether CoQ10 supplements consistently help. Discuss persistent muscle symptoms with your prescriber, and do not stop a statin on your own.
depletions.monitoring_note: Routine blood CoQ10 testing is not part of standard care; persistent muscle symptoms are assessed clinically.

depletions.alert_body: With long-term PPI use, reduced stomach acid may lower absorption of vitamin B12 from food. Not everyone develops low levels.
depletions.acknowledgement_note: You're already considering B12 intake; testing and individual factors still guide whether treatment is needed.
depletions.monitoring_tip_short: Ask whether B12 testing fits if use is prolonged or anemia, nerve symptoms, or other factors appear.

depletions.mechanism: Rare PPI-associated hypomagnesemia appears to involve reduced intestinal magnesium absorption, but the precise molecular mechanism is not established. Dechallenge and rechallenge reports support a PPI class effect.
depletions.clinical_impact: Low magnesium may be asymptomatic or can contribute to tetany, seizures, or arrhythmias and may accompany low calcium or potassium. FDA labeling notes that some cases required magnesium replacement and stopping the PPI.
depletions.recommendation: Do not start a routine magnesium dose solely because you take a PPI. For prolonged therapy—especially with digoxin, a diuretic, or other risk factors—ask whether baseline and periodic magnesium testing is appropriate. Management of a low result should be clinician-directed.
depletions.monitoring_note: FDA labeling advises considering magnesium before and periodically during prolonged PPI therapy, especially with digoxin or medicines that can lower magnesium.

depletions.alert_headline: Rarely, long-term PPIs may lower magnesium

depletions.acknowledgement_note: You're already tracking magnesium intake; laboratory results and your treatment plan guide any needed changes.

depletions.mechanism: PPIs reduce stomach acid. In fasting studies this can reduce absorption of insoluble calcium carbonate; calcium citrate is less acid-dependent, and taking carbonate with food improves absorption. This does not establish whole-body calcium deficiency.
depletions.clinical_impact: Long-term PPI use is associated in observational studies with a modestly higher fracture risk, but confounding remains and the association does not prove calcium deficiency.
depletions.recommendation: Do not start calcium solely because you take a PPI. Aim for adequate dietary calcium and vitamin D. If a clinician recommends calcium, ask whether calcium citrate or calcium carbonate taken with food fits your situation.
depletions.monitoring_note: Consider DEXA scan for bone density assessment with long-term PPI use, especially postmenopausal women.

depletions.alert_body: With long-term use, PPIs can reduce fasting absorption of calcium carbonate, but they do not automatically cause calcium deficiency.

depletions.mechanism: Gastric acid helps release non-heme iron from food and supports its absorption. PPIs and H2 blockers suppress acid, so long-term use can lower non-heme iron absorption. In the observational study, the association with iron deficiency became weaker after acid-suppressing treatment was discontinued. This does not mean that an existing deficiency will always reverse after stopping treatment.
depletions.clinical_impact: Use for two years or longer is associated with a higher risk of iron deficiency. The association was stronger for PPIs than H2 blockers; among PPI users, it increased with higher doses and longer duration. Other causes of iron deficiency still need clinical evaluation.
depletions.recommendation: If you use a PPI or H2 blocker long term and have iron-deficiency symptoms or risk factors, ask your clinician whether ferritin and blood-count testing is appropriate. Do not start iron without confirming the cause and a suitable treatment plan, and do not stop the acid reducer on your own.
depletions.monitoring_note: Testing is symptom- and risk-based; ask whether ferritin and a blood count are appropriate during prolonged acid-suppressing treatment.

depletions.alert_body: PPI or H2-blocker use for two years or longer is associated with iron deficiency; the association was stronger for PPIs.
depletions.acknowledgement_note: You're taking iron — a thoughtful step while using acid-reducing medication long-term.
depletions.monitoring_tip_short: Discuss ferritin and blood-count testing if long-term use coincides with symptoms or other iron-deficiency risks.
depletions.food_sources_short: Food sources of iron include red meat, poultry, seafood, beans, lentils, tofu, spinach, and fortified cereals.

depletions.mechanism: The acidic gastric environment normally stabilizes vitamin C (ascorbic acid). Elevated gastric pH from acid suppression accelerates oxidation of ascorbic acid to dehydroascorbic acid, reducing its bioavailability. Gastric secretion of vitamin C is also reduced.
depletions.clinical_impact: Mild vitamin C depletion may impair immune function, collagen synthesis, and antioxidant defenses. The clinical significance is generally modest in individuals with adequate dietary intake.
depletions.recommendation: Ensure adequate vitamin C intake from fruits and vegetables. If supplementing, take vitamin C away from antacid doses to minimize pH-related degradation.

depletions.alert_headline: May modestly affect vitamin C over time
depletions.alert_body: Higher stomach pH from acid-reducers can gradually reduce how well vitamin C holds up through digestion. The effect is typically modest with regular use.
depletions.acknowledgement_note: Nice — your vitamin C intake supports levels while using acid-reducing medication.
depletions.monitoring_tip_short: Consider taking vitamin C at a different time of day from acid-reducing medication.
depletions.food_sources_short: Food sources of vitamin C include citrus fruits, strawberries, bell peppers, broccoli, kiwi, and tomatoes.
depletions.citation_review_note: Rejected as a consumer depletion warning (evidence-based, not a data gap). Only one small systemic study (Henry 2005: omeprazole 40 mg x 4 wk → plasma vitamin C -12.3%, authors state 'clinical significance is unclear', concentrated in H. pylori+/low-baseline). The remaining literature is intragastric gastric-juice ascorbate (an N-nitrosation/cancer mechanism, not body vitamin C status). No clinically meaningful depletion; no H2/antacid data. Retired the Pelton handbook citation.

depletions.mechanism: Zinc absorption from food is partially dependent on gastric acid solubilization. Elevated gastric pH impairs the release of zinc from food-bound complexes, reducing bioavailability of dietary zinc.
depletions.clinical_impact: Zinc deficiency affects immune function, wound healing, taste and smell, and reproductive health. Long-term marginal zinc depletion is most concerning in elderly patients with already-borderline intake.
depletions.recommendation: Ensure dietary zinc adequacy. If on long-term antacids, consider a modest zinc supplement (10–15 mg/day as zinc glycinate). Avoid taking zinc simultaneously with the acid-reducing medication.

depletions.alert_headline: May slightly lower zinc over time
depletions.alert_body: With long-term use, acid-reducing medications can gradually reduce how well zinc is freed from food and absorbed. The effect is usually mild.
depletions.acknowledgement_note: Good — your zinc intake helps support levels while on acid-reducing medication.
depletions.monitoring_tip_short: Consider taking zinc at a different time of day from acid-reducing medication.
depletions.food_sources_short: Food sources of zinc include oysters, meat, poultry, beans, lentils, nuts, seeds, and whole grains.
depletions.citation_review_note: Rejected as a consumer depletion warning (evidence-based, not a data gap). Support exists only for reduced acute absorption of a fasting soluble zinc-salt load (H2: Sturniolo 1991; PPI: Ozutemiz 2002) — a supplement-timing pharmacokinetic effect. A food-based study (Serfaty-Lacrosniere 1995) found NO change in zinc absorption from a meal, and no study shows actual zinc deficiency from acid suppression. Retired the Pelton handbook citation.

depletions.mechanism: Metformin can reduce vitamin B12 absorption through a multifactorial process. Reduced calcium-dependent uptake of the intrinsic-factor–B12 complex in the ileum is one proposed mechanism, but it is not the only established explanation.
depletions.clinical_impact: The chance of low vitamin B12 rises with higher metformin dose, longer treatment, and other B12 risk factors. Deficiency can cause anemia or neuropathy, which can be mistaken for diabetic neuropathy.
depletions.recommendation: Consider periodic vitamin B12 assessment during long-term metformin use, especially with higher doses, symptoms of deficiency, or other B12 risk factors. Treat confirmed deficiency with clinician guidance; do not stop metformin on your own.
depletions.monitoring_note: Consider periodic vitamin B12 assessment in people taking metformin, particularly with anemia, neuropathy symptoms, higher doses, longer treatment duration, or other deficiency risk factors. Methylmalonic acid is a sensitive functional marker for early deficiency.

depletions.mechanism: Estrogen components of OCPs impair folate metabolism and reduce serum folate levels. The mechanism involves altered folate binding protein expression and possibly impaired intestinal folate absorption.

depletions.recommendation: Take a daily multivitamin with 400–800 mcg folate (methylfolate preferred) throughout OCP use. This is especially critical for anyone who may become pregnant after stopping.
depletions.monitoring_note: Consider starting 5-methyltetrahydrofolate supplementation at least 3 months before attempting conception after stopping OCPs.

depletions.mechanism: Loop and thiazide diuretics increase renal sodium delivery and urinary electrolyte losses. This can lower potassium; the likelihood depends on the agent, dose, intake, kidney function, and concurrent medications.
depletions.clinical_impact: Low potassium can cause muscle weakness or cramps and increase arrhythmia risk; it can also increase digoxin toxicity. Some patients do not develop low potassium, and kidney disease or other medicines can instead raise it.

depletions.monitoring_note: Monitor serum potassium at intervals chosen for the specific diuretic, dose, kidney function, intercurrent illness, and interacting medicines.

depletions.alert_headline: Loop and thiazide diuretics may lower potassium
depletions.alert_body: With regular use or after dose changes, loop and thiazide diuretics can lower potassium. The effect varies and laboratory monitoring guides management.
depletions.acknowledgement_note: Confirm any potassium product—including over-the-counter—with your prescriber; the right amount depends on your labs.
depletions.monitoring_tip_short: Ask how often potassium should be checked based on the diuretic, dose, kidneys, and other medicines.
depletions.food_sources_short: Potassium is found in potatoes, beans, fruit, dairy, and vegetables; whether to change intake depends on labs and kidney function.
depletions.citation_review_note: B1.1 evidence revision completed. Current furosemide and hydrochlorothiazide labels support hypokalemia and electrolyte monitoring across the existing loop/thiazide-only class. depletions.mechanism: Loop and thiazide diuretics can increase urinary magnesium losses through their effects on renal electrolyte handling. The magnitude and mechanism differ by diuretic subclass and by individual clinical factors.
depletions.clinical_impact: Low magnesium can contribute to weakness, cramps, tremor, or arrhythmias and can coexist with low potassium. The finding requires clinical interpretation because symptoms and risk also depend on kidney function and other medicines.
depletions.recommendation: Do not start a routine magnesium dose solely because you take a diuretic. Ask whether magnesium should be included with electrolyte monitoring, especially if potassium is low, symptoms appear, the dose is high, or intake is limited; correction should be clinician-directed.
depletions.monitoring_note: Use periodic or more frequent electrolyte monitoring according to the specific agent, dose, kidney function, symptoms, and other medicines; include magnesium when clinically relevant.

depletions.mechanism: Thiazide diuretics increase urinary zinc excretion; loop diuretics have a much smaller effect. Over long-term use this can modestly lower tissue zinc, although blood zinc usually remains in the normal range.

depletions.mechanism: Loop diuretics (furosemide, bumetanide, torsemide) inhibit the NKCC2 transporter in the thick ascending limb, which is also needed for calcium reabsorption, so more calcium is lost in the urine. Thiazide diuretics do the opposite and retain calcium.
depletions.clinical_impact: Long-term loop-diuretic use is linked to a modestly higher fracture risk, mainly in older adults, and part of that may reflect falls rather than bone loss alone. It is a modest effect and does not by itself mean a calcium shortfall.
depletions.recommendation: If you take a loop diuretic long-term, aim for adequate dietary calcium and vitamin D and ask your doctor about bone health. Most people do not need high-dose calcium supplements.

depletions.mechanism: Triamterene is a structural analog of folate and a weak inhibitor of dihydrofolate reductase, the enzyme that activates folate. At usual doses cells largely compensate, so the effect on folate status is modest.
depletions.clinical_impact: For most folate-replete people at normal doses, meaningful folate depletion is uncommon. depletions.recommendation: Most people on triamterene do not need a folate supplement. If you are pregnant, planning pregnancy, have low folate, or take methotrexate, discuss folate with your doctor.
depletions.monitoring_note: Check serum folate and homocysteine in patients on long-term triamterene therapy.

depletions.mechanism: Long-term oral prednisone can reduce intestinal calcium absorption, increase urinary calcium loss, reduce bone formation, and increase bone resorption. The concern is bone strength rather than a measurable fall in blood calcium.
depletions.clinical_impact: Prednisone taken for more than three months at about 2.5 mg/day or more raises osteoporosis and fracture risk. Short courses are not represented by this record.
depletions.recommendation: For prednisone expected to continue longer than three months, clinicians assess calcium and vitamin D intake, fracture risk, and whether bone-protective treatment is needed. Care is based on individual risk rather than an automatic supplement dose.
depletions.monitoring_note: American College of Rheumatology guidance recommends assessing fracture risk soon after starting long-term glucocorticoids — clinical fracture assessment, bone mineral density with vertebral fracture assessment, and FRAX scoring for adults 40 and older.

depletions.mechanism: SSRIs are associated with SIADH and dilutional hyponatremia, in which excess water lowers blood sodium. Serotonergic effects on antidiuretic hormone are proposed, but the exact mechanism is not fully established.
depletions.clinical_impact: Risk is highest soon after starting an SSRI and in older adults, people taking thiazide diuretics, and those with prior hyponatremia. Severe hyponatremia can cause marked confusion, seizures, or reduced consciousness.
depletions.recommendation: If you have hyponatremia risk factors, your prescriber may check sodium at baseline and during early treatment. Report new nausea, headache, unsteadiness, or confusion promptly; seizures or reduced consciousness require urgent care. This is not treated by self-supplementing sodium. Do not stop or change your antidepressant on your own. Contact your prescriber.
depletions.monitoring_note: Monitoring decisions and timing should be individualized, especially soon after starting therapy in older adults, people taking diuretics, or those with prior hyponatremia.

depletions.mechanism: The pregnancy literature on enzyme-inducing antiseizure medications and vitamin K is mixed. depletions.mechanism: Calcium supplements and calcium-containing medicines can bind levothyroxine in the gastrointestinal tract and reduce its absorption. This affects thyroid-drug bioavailability rather than depleting body calcium stores.
depletions.clinical_impact: In 20 patients with hypothyroidism, taking 1,200 mg/day of elemental calcium as calcium carbonate with levothyroxine for three months increased mean TSH from 1.6 to 2.7 mIU/L; 20% had TSH above the normal range. Calcium can therefore reduce thyroid-drug absorption and lead to inadequate control in some patients.
depletions.recommendation: Take calcium supplements and calcium-containing medicines at least 4 hours before or after levothyroxine. Continue taking levothyroxine on an empty stomach, normally 30 to 60 minutes before breakfast. The 4-hour rule applies to calcium supplements and medicines; ask your clinician if you are unsure how your usual meals fit around it.
depletions.monitoring_note: Ask whether TSH should be rechecked after starting, stopping, or changing the timing or dose of calcium supplements or calcium-containing medicines.

depletions.mechanism: Iron supplements can bind levothyroxine in the gut and reduce its absorption. In a small uncontrolled 12-week study of 14 patients with hypothyroidism, taking a 300 mg ferrous sulfate tablet with levothyroxine raised mean TSH from 1.6 to 5.4 mIU/L.
depletions.clinical_impact: Co-administration can lead to inadequate thyroid hormone levels and a return of hypothyroid symptoms; the effect is variable but clinically significant in some patients.
depletions.recommendation: Take iron supplements at least 4 hours before or after levothyroxine. If you start or stop iron, ask your clinician about rechecking your thyroid levels.
depletions.monitoring_note: Check TSH within 6–8 weeks of starting iron supplementation in levothyroxine-treated patients. Separate administration times by at least 4 hours.

depletions.mechanism: High-dose folic acid supplementation may compete with zinc for intestinal absorption via shared transport mechanisms. This interaction is most relevant when very high folic acid doses (>5 mg/day) are taken without balanced mineral supplementation.
depletions.clinical_impact: In populations with already marginal zinc intake (elderly, pregnant women), high folic acid could theoretically reduce zinc absorption enough to impair immune function and growth outcomes. Clinical significance at typical supplement doses (400–800 mcg) is low.
depletions.recommendation: At standard supplemental doses, this interaction is not clinically significant. For those taking high-dose folic acid (>5 mg/day), ensure zinc intake from dietary sources or a balanced multivitamin.

depletions.alert_headline: High-dose folate may affect zinc uptake

depletions.monitoring_tip_short: Consider a balanced multivitamin rather than high single-nutrient doses; check with your clinician.
depletions.food_sources_short: Food sources of zinc include meat, poultry, shellfish, beans, lentils, nuts, seeds, and whole grains.

depletions.mechanism: Isoniazid binds and inactivates pyridoxal phosphate, the active coenzyme form of vitamin B6, and increases urinary loss of pyridoxine metabolites. This can lower functional B6 status during tuberculosis therapy.
depletions.clinical_impact: Low vitamin B6 during isoniazid therapy can contribute to peripheral neuropathy, tingling, burning sensations, and rarely anemia or neuropsychiatric symptoms. Higher-risk patients are often supplemented from the start.
depletions.recommendation: Pyridoxine is commonly used with isoniazid, especially in people at higher neuropathy risk. Confirm the exact dose with the clinician managing tuberculosis therapy.
depletions.monitoring_note: Ask about pyridoxine co-therapy if isoniazid is used long term or if neuropathy symptoms appear.

depletions.mechanism: Methotrexate is an antifolate medicine. With low-dose regimens for inflammatory disease, clinician-prescribed folic or folinic acid can reduce folate-mediated adverse effects. Oncology and rescue regimens use different folate protocols.
depletions.clinical_impact: In low-dose inflammatory-disease treatment, appropriate folate support can reduce mouth sores, nausea, liver-enzyme elevations, cytopenias, and treatment discontinuation. The schedule cannot be generalized to cancer treatment.
depletions.recommendation: Use only the folic-acid or folinic-acid schedule prescribed for your exact methotrexate regimen. Do not start, stop, or retime folate without the rheumatology, dermatology, gastroenterology, or oncology prescriber.
depletions.monitoring_note: Review folate schedule, CBC, and liver-enzyme monitoring with the methotrexate prescriber.

depletions.alert_body: With regular use, folate support is common for low-dose methotrexate in inflammatory disease, but oncology regimens differ.
depletions.acknowledgement_note: Good — folate intake is worth tracking while your clinician manages methotrexate therapy.
depletions.monitoring_tip_short: Consider confirming your exact folic-acid schedule with the clinician who prescribes methotrexate.

depletions.mechanism: Orlistat inhibits gastrointestinal lipases and reduces absorption of dietary fat. Because Vitamin A is fat-soluble, lower fat absorption can reduce uptake unless vitamin intake is separated from the orlistat dose.
depletions.clinical_impact: Orlistat can lower absorption of fat-soluble vitamins, so its label recommends a daily multivitamin. Orlistat is not for use during pregnancy; this is a medication-safety issue, not a vitamin-dose adjustment. Separately, excess preformed vitamin A can cause birth defects.
depletions.recommendation: Take the daily multivitamin recommended in the orlistat label—containing vitamins A, D, E, and K plus beta-carotene—at least 2 hours before or after orlistat, such as at bedtime. Do not add extra vitamin A unless your clinician recommends it. Orlistat is not for use during pregnancy. If you are pregnant or think you may be pregnant, contact the prescriber before taking another dose.
depletions.monitoring_note: Check Vitamin A status if orlistat is used long term or if fat-soluble vitamin intake is low.

depletions.monitoring_tip_short: Ask the prescriber before another dose if pregnancy is possible; take the multivitamin 2 hours apart.

depletions.mechanism: Sulfasalazine can inhibit intestinal absorption and metabolism of folic acid. This can lower functional folate availability during long-term treatment, especially when baseline folate intake is marginal.
depletions.clinical_impact: Lower folate status can contribute to mouth soreness, anemia, elevated homocysteine, and pregnancy-related neural tube risk. This matters most with long-term therapy or pregnancy planning.
depletions.recommendation: Folate support should be clinician-directed with sulfasalazine, especially before pregnancy or during long-term use. Confirm the form and dose with the prescriber.
depletions.monitoring_note: Review folate status and pregnancy planning needs with the clinician managing sulfasalazine.

depletions.mechanism: Colchicine can affect intestinal mucosal function and has been listed among medicines associated with vitamin B12 malabsorption. Long-term use may reduce B12 uptake in susceptible people.
depletions.clinical_impact: Long-term colchicine can contribute to low B12 in susceptible people, but modern evidence does not establish deficiency or routine screening in every user. Symptoms and other B12 risks should guide evaluation.
depletions.recommendation: If long-term colchicine use coincides with anemia, neuropathy symptoms, or other B12 risk factors, ask whether B12 testing is appropriate. Routine supplementation is not established solely because colchicine is prescribed.
depletions.monitoring_note: Ask about B12 testing if colchicine is used chronically or if neuropathy symptoms develop.

depletions.mechanism: Cholestyramine binds bile acids in the gut and can interfere with fat digestion and absorption. Because Vitamin A is fat-soluble, long-term bile-acid binding can reduce absorption unless vitamin timing is managed.
depletions.clinical_impact: Long-term cholestyramine use can lower vitamin A absorption. Excess preformed vitamin A can cause birth defects, so pregnancy or possible pregnancy requires clinician review of the vitamin A form and total dose.
depletions.recommendation: For long-term use, ask whether a water-miscible vitamin A form is appropriate. The label directs other medicines at least 1 hour before or 4–6 hours after cholestyramine; confirm how to time the vitamin. If you are pregnant or could become pregnant, have the vitamin A form and total dose reviewed rather than adding extra preformed vitamin A.
depletions.monitoring_note: Consider Vitamin A monitoring during long-term or high-dose cholestyramine therapy.
